lessons.title: Lesson 1: The QuickBooks bookkeeper job and the path to it
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the main duties of a QuickBooks bookkeeper and name a credential that can help you get hired.
This lesson builds toward: Given a bookkeeping job posting or a client request, you will list the main duties of a QuickBooks bookkeeper and name an Intuit credential that fits the job, naming at least four duties and the official page where the credential is checked.
A bookkeeper records a business's money so the owner always knows where it stands. In QuickBooks that means: sending invoices and recording customer payments, entering bills and expenses, reviewing the bank feed, reconciling the bank each month, running reports, and keeping receipts. Bookkeepers work for one company, for an accounting firm, or for several small clients as their own business. Churches and nonprofits need them too.
QuickBooks Online is Intuit's web version, used in a browser. QuickBooks Desktop is installed on a computer. Most new small business customers use QuickBooks Online, so this course uses it, but the ideas are the same in both.
Two Intuit credentials fit this course. The QuickBooks Certified User shows you can use QuickBooks. The Intuit Certified Bookkeeping Professional shows you know bookkeeping basics. Both exams are delivered by Certiport, a Pearson VUE business, and Intuit Academy offers training. Accountants can also earn QuickBooks ProAdvisor certification. This course prepares you; it does not grant any credential. Fees, eligibility and exam details change, so check the official pages.
A bookkeeper is not a tax preparer or a certified public accountant (CPA). You keep the records clean; tax questions go to a tax professional or irs.gov.
Words to know:
- Bookkeeper: a person who records a business's money in and money out and keeps the records accurate.
- QuickBooks Online: Intuit's bookkeeping software that runs in a web browser.
- Credential: a certificate that shows you passed an official exam.
- Certiport: a Pearson VUE company that delivers Intuit's certification exams.
- CPA: a certified public accountant: a licensed accountant who can do work a bookkeeper cannot, such as audits.
Official sources:
- Certiport (Pearson VUE): Intuit certifications, including QuickBooks Certified User and Intuit Certified Bookkeeping Professional
- Intuit Academy (Intuit's training and certification site)
- QuickBooks ProAdvisor training and certification (for accountants)
Try it now: Find one bookkeeping job posting online (search "bookkeeper QuickBooks" on a job site). Write down four duties it lists and whether it asks for a QuickBooks credential. Then open the Certiport page in the sources and write the names of the two Intuit credentials that fit.
You can now list what a QuickBooks bookkeeper does and name a credential that fits the job.

check.q: Which task is part of a bookkeeper's monthly work?
options: Signing the company's tax return as a CPA
check.why: Reconciling the bank each month is core bookkeeping work.

check.q: Who delivers the QuickBooks Certified User exam?
check.why: Certiport, a Pearson VUE business, delivers Intuit's certification exams.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The chart of accounts and two-sided entries
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Sort a business's money activity into the five types of accounts.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of a small business's money activity, you will sort each item into the right type of account in a chart of accounts, placing at least 9 of 10 items in the right account type.
The chart of accounts is the list of every place money can be sorted in QuickBooks. Each account belongs to one of five types. Income: money earned, like sales or donations. Expenses: costs of running the business, like supplies, rent and fuel. Assets: things the business owns or is owed, like the bank account, equipment and money customers still owe. Liabilities: money the business owes, like a loan, a credit card or bills not yet paid. Equity: the owner's share, including money the owner put in or took out.
Every entry touches at least two accounts. That is called double-entry bookkeeping. When you send a $200 invoice, income goes up and the money customers owe you (accounts receivable) goes up. When the customer pays, accounts receivable goes down and the bank goes up. QuickBooks does the second side for you when you use the right form, which is why choosing the right form and account matters.
QuickBooks gives every new company a starting chart of accounts based on the type of business. A bookkeeper cleans it up: adds accounts the business really uses, renames vague ones, and keeps names the same every month. A nonprofit might add accounts like Donations, Grants and Program supplies.
In the test drive, search for "chart of accounts" to open the list and see each account's type.
Step by step:
- Open the chart of accounts (search for it if you cannot find it).
- Read the type of each account: income, expense, asset, liability or equity.
- Add the accounts the business really uses.
- Rename vague accounts so anyone can understand them.
- Use the same account every time for the same kind of money.
Words to know:
- Chart of accounts: the list of every account money can be sorted into.
- Asset: something the business owns or is owed, like cash in the bank or equipment.
- Liability: money the business owes, like a loan or an unpaid bill.
- Equity: the owner's share of the business.
- Accounts receivable (A/R): money customers owe the business.
- Accounts payable (A/P): money the business owes to vendors for bills not yet paid.
- Double-entry: every entry changes at least two accounts so the books stay in balance.
Try it now: On paper, make two columns: Item and Account type. Sort these ten items: cleaning supplies, money in the business checking account, a customer who owes $150, a truck loan, sales of cleaning services, the owner putting in $500 to start, rent, a credit card balance, a donated grant (for a nonprofit), and a new vacuum. Then open the chart of accounts in the test drive and compare how the sample company sorts similar items.
You can now sort money activity into income, expense, asset, liability and equity accounts.

check.q: A business owes $3,000 on a truck loan. What type of account is the loan?
check.why: Money the business owes is a liability.

check.q: Money customers still owe the business is tracked in:
check.why: Accounts receivable (A/R) is money customers owe.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Invoices, sales receipts and customer payments
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Record an invoice, a sales receipt and a customer payment in QuickBooks.
This lesson builds toward: Given a sale, a customer and a payment, you will record the invoice or sales receipt and the customer payment in QuickBooks, with the right customer, date, amount and income account, and no invoice left open after it is paid.
Use an invoice when the customer pays later. The invoice lists the customer, date, products or services, amount and due date. Use a sales receipt when the customer pays at the time of the sale, like a food truck sale. Both record income; only the invoice creates money owed (accounts receivable).
When an invoice is paid, record the payment against that invoice. Do not create a new sale, or the income will be counted twice. QuickBooks then marks the invoice paid. If the customer paid by cash or check, QuickBooks may hold the payment until you record the bank deposit, so the deposit matches what the bank shows.
Set up each customer once with their name and contact details, and set up each product or service once with its price and income account. Then every invoice uses the same accounts.
In QuickBooks Online, new forms like invoices, sales receipts and payments start from the New (+) button. In the test drive, nothing is saved, so write down what you entered.
Step by step:
- Choose the form: invoice (pay later) or sales receipt (paid now).
- Pick the customer, or add a new one.
- Enter the date, the product or service, the amount and the due date.
- Save the form.
- When the customer pays an invoice, record the payment against that invoice.
- Record the bank deposit if QuickBooks holds the payment to deposit later.
- Check that the invoice now shows as paid.
Words to know:
- Invoice: a bill you send a customer who will pay later.
- Sales receipt: a record of a sale paid at the time of the sale.
- Customer payment: the record that a customer paid an invoice.
- Deposit: money put into the bank, which should match the bank statement.
Official sources:
- Intuit QuickBooks help: Test drive and practice using QuickBooks Online
Try it now: Open the QuickBooks Online test drive (link in the sources; open it in a private browser window). Create an invoice for $250 of landscaping services to a sample customer, due in 30 days. Then receive a payment for that invoice and check that the invoice shows as paid. Write the customer, date, amount and income account on paper, because the test drive does not save. No computer? Draw the invoice and the payment on paper.
You can now record an invoice, a sales receipt and a customer payment so income is counted once.

check.q: A food truck customer pays at the window. Which form do you use?
check.why: A sales receipt records a sale paid at the time of the sale.

check.q: A customer pays a $250 invoice. What do you record?
check.why: Recording the payment against the invoice closes it without counting income twice.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Bills, the bank and the month-end

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Bills, expenses and vendors
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Enter a bill, an expense and a bill payment with the right vendor and account.
This lesson builds toward: Given a bill, a receipt and a vendor, you will enter the bill, the expense and the bill payment in QuickBooks, with the right vendor, date, amount and expense account, and the receipt attached or noted.
A vendor is anyone the business buys from: the supply store, the landlord, the phone company. Set up each vendor once.
Use a bill when the business will pay later, like a supplier invoice due in 30 days. The bill goes into accounts payable. When you pay it, record a bill payment against that bill so it is not counted twice. Use an expense when the business pays right away, like a card purchase at the hardware store.
Choose the expense account that matches what was bought: Supplies, Fuel, Rent, Phone. Attach a photo of the receipt in QuickBooks, or write the receipt number in the memo. Receipts back up every expense if anyone asks later.
If the business pays contractors, collect a Form W-9 from each one before paying and mark them as contractors, because some businesses must file information returns for them. The rules and dollar amounts change, so check irs.gov or a tax professional.
Step by step:
- Pick the vendor, or add a new one.
- Choose bill (pay later) or expense (paid now).
- Enter the date, amount and the matching expense account.
- Attach the receipt or note its number.
- When you pay a bill, record a bill payment against that bill.
- Check that the bill now shows as paid.
Words to know:
- Vendor: a person or business the business buys from.
- Bill: a record of something the business will pay for later.
- Expense: a record of something the business paid for right away.
- Bill payment: the record that a bill was paid.
- Form W-9: an IRS form a contractor fills out with their name and tax number for the business's records.
Official sources:
- IRS: About Form W-9
- Intuit QuickBooks help: Test drive and practice using QuickBooks Online
Try it now: In the test drive or on paper, enter three items: a $120 supply bill due in 30 days, a $45 fuel purchase paid by card today, and the payment of the $120 bill two weeks later. For each, write the vendor, the form you used, the account and the amount. Then explain in one sentence why the bill payment is not a new expense.
You can now enter bills, expenses and bill payments with the right vendor, account and receipt.

check.q: A supplier sends a bill due in 30 days. What do you enter today?
check.why: A bill records something the business will pay later.

check.q: You pay that bill two weeks later. What do you record?
options: A new expense for the same amount
A bill payment against that bill
check.why: A bill payment closes the bill without counting the cost twice.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The bank feed and the bank reconciliation
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Match bank feed lines to entries and reconcile the bank account to a difference of zero.
This lesson builds toward: Given a month of bank activity and a bank statement, you will match the bank feed and reconcile the bank account, ending with a difference of zero, or a written note of what is still off.
QuickBooks can connect to the business's bank and download its transactions. That is the bank feed. Each downloaded line waits for you to review it. If you already entered it, match it to that entry. If not, add it with the right payee and account. Never add a line that is already entered, or it will count twice. The business owner connects the bank; a bookkeeper never asks for the owner's bank password.
A bank reconciliation proves that QuickBooks agrees with the bank statement. Once a month, take the statement, enter its ending balance and date, and tick each deposit and payment in QuickBooks that is on the statement. When the difference is zero, finish the reconciliation.
If the difference is not zero, look for the usual causes: a bank fee or interest not entered, an entry typed with the wrong amount, a duplicate, or an entry in the wrong month. Checks that have not cleared yet stay unticked; they will clear next month.
Never force a reconciliation to zero by making up an entry. If you cannot find the problem, write a note and ask the owner or an accountant.
Step by step:
- Review each new bank feed line.
- Match it to an existing entry, or add it with the right payee and account.
- Get the month's bank statement.
- Start a reconciliation and enter the statement's ending date and balance.
- Tick each entry that appears on the statement.
- Find and fix anything that keeps the difference from zero.
- Finish when the difference is zero, or write a note and ask for help.
Words to know:
- Bank feed: bank transactions that QuickBooks downloads for you to review.
- Match: linking a downloaded bank line to an entry already in QuickBooks.
- Reconcile: check that your records agree with the bank statement, line by line.
- Difference: the gap between QuickBooks and the bank statement during a reconciliation; it should be zero.
- Uncleared check: a check you wrote that the bank has not paid yet.
Official sources:
- Intuit QuickBooks help: Test drive and practice using QuickBooks Online
Try it now: Make a practice statement on paper: starting balance $1,000; deposits $250 and $400; payments $120, $45 and $60; a $5 bank fee; ending balance $1,420. Your book record has every line except the bank fee, plus a $75 check that has not cleared. Tick the matching lines, find what keeps the difference from zero, and write what you would enter. In the test drive, open the banking page and look at how downloaded lines wait to be matched or added.
You can now match the bank feed and reconcile a bank account to a difference of zero, or write down what is still off.

check.q: A bank feed line is a payment you already entered as a bill payment. What do you do?
options: Match it to that bill payment
Add it as a new expense
check.why: Matching links the bank line to your entry without counting it twice.

check.q: Your reconciliation is off by $5, and the statement shows a $5 bank fee. What is the best step?
options: Make up an entry for any amount
Enter the $5 bank fee as an expense
check.why: A missing bank fee is a common cause; entering it fixes the difference honestly.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Reports and the month-end close
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Run and explain the profit and loss, the balance sheet and the open invoices report.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of a month, you will run and explain the profit and loss, the balance sheet and the open invoices report, stating the month's profit or loss and who still owes money.
The profit and loss (P&L) shows income minus expenses for a period, like one month. If income is bigger, the business made a profit; if expenses are bigger, it had a loss. The balance sheet shows, on one date, what the business has (assets), what it owes (liabilities) and the owner's share (equity).
The accounts receivable aging report shows which customers still owe money and how late they are. The accounts payable aging report shows which bills the business still owes. These two reports tell the owner whom to call and what to pay next.
A month-end close is the checklist a bookkeeper follows each month: all sales, payments, bills and expenses entered; the bank feed reviewed; every bank and credit card account reconciled; receipts attached; reports run and sent to the owner with a short note. Nonprofits may also run reports by program or grant.
Run reports from the Reports area; search for the report by name. A report is only as good as the entries behind it, so reconcile first.
Step by step:
- Finish entering the month's sales, payments, bills and expenses.
- Review the bank feed and reconcile every bank and card account.
- Run the profit and loss for the month.
- Run the balance sheet for the last day of the month.
- Run the accounts receivable aging report.
- Write the owner a short note: profit or loss, who owes money and bills due soon.
Words to know:
- Profit and loss (P&L): a report of income minus expenses for a period; also called an income statement.
- Balance sheet: a report of assets, liabilities and equity on one date.
- Aging report: a report of money owed, sorted by how many days late it is.
- Month-end close: the checklist that finishes the books for a month.
Official sources:
- Intuit QuickBooks help: Test drive and practice using QuickBooks Online
Try it now: In the test drive, run the profit and loss for last month and the accounts receivable aging report. Write three sentences for the owner: the month's total income and total expenses, whether there was a profit or a loss, and which customer owes the most. No computer? Use your work from the earlier lessons and write the same note on paper.
You can now run the main reports, explain them to an owner and close a month.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Chart of accounts Fewer than 12 accounts, or several are marked with the wrong type. At least 12 accounts, each with the right type, with clear names. Also explains why each account is needed for this business, including nonprofit or industry accounts. Sales and payments A payment was recorded as a new sale, or an invoice is missing a customer, date or amount. At least 3 invoices and 2 payments, each with customer, date, amount and income account; paid invoices show as paid. Also records the bank deposit for each payment and notes which invoices are still open. Bills and expenses A bill was paid with a new expense, or entries have no account or receipt. At least 4 bills or expenses with vendor, date, amount, account and receipt noted. Also shows a bill payment and a contractor set up with a W-9 note. Bank reconciliation No reconciliation, or it was forced to zero with a made-up entry. Reconciliation ends at a difference of zero, or has an honest note of what is still off. Also lists what caused each difference (fee, typo, duplicate, uncleared check) and how it was fixed. Report summary The summary is missing the profit or loss, or the numbers do not match the entries. States total income, total expenses and the profit or loss, and who still owes money. Also names bills due soon and one thing the owner could act on. Credential plan No credential named, or no dates. Names an Intuit credential, the official page to check and dates for checking it and for practice tests. Also lists three employers or clients to contact and a date to contact each. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which report shows whether the business made money last month?
check.why: The profit and loss shows income minus expenses for a period.

check.q: The owner asks which customers are late paying. Which report do you run?
check.why: The A/R aging report lists customers who owe money and how late they are.
